title: The Water and the Table
subtitle: A five-session study on baptism and the Lord's Supper, on why God gives his people physical signs, and on the water and the meal that mark and feed the church.
summary:
This study is for new believers, membership classes, small groups, and any Christian who has taken the water and the bread for years without ever stopping to ask what they are. It walks slowly through five sessions on why Christianity, of all the world's faiths, refuses to be only a matter of the mind and insists on things you can touch, on baptism and the long, honest disagreement between those who baptize believers and those who baptize their infant children, on what baptism says about who you now are, buried and raised with Christ, on the range of ways faithful Christians have understood what happens at the Lord's table, and on the meal that was given to make a divided people one. It is built so a volunteer with no seminary training can lead it. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every contested point is stated in its strongest form before any verdict lands.

This is not a study that pretends the differences are not real, and it is not a study that treats them as walls. The writer is a Baptist pastor, and he says so plainly, and he still means to state the paedobaptist case and the range of views on the table so honestly that a thoughtful believer from the other side would finish feeling understood rather than beaten. He came to faith from atheism, carrying the modern instinct that the real world is only the world you can measure and that religion is something private and invisible, and he writes as a man the water and the table had to teach that God saves creatures with bodies through the good stuff of a world he made. The one thing this study will not do is let a second-order disagreement about the timing of a baptism or the metaphysics of a supper become the thing that divides the one body Christ died to make one. The mode of the water and the meaning of the meal are worth studying, worth deciding, worth holding with conviction. They were never worth breaking the table over.
audience: New believers, membership and baptism classes, and small groups of any tradition

sessions.title: Why God Gave Us Water and Bread
sessions.aim: To see why Christianity refuses to be a religion only of the mind and insists on physical signs, to ground the sacraments in the goodness of the created world and the flesh God took on in Christ, and to hold together, without a fight, the traditions that say sacrament and the traditions that say ordinance.
sessions.summary: A man sat in Bell's study who had followed Jesus for a decade and never been baptized, and when Bell asked why, the man said he did not see the point of getting wet, that his faith was inward, a thing of the heart and the mind, and that the water and the bread struck him as leftover religion for people who needed props. Bell says he understood the instinct completely, because he came to faith from atheism carrying the same conviction the whole culture carries, that the real world is the world you can measure and that anything holy must be invisible and private. The real question is why Christianity, which could have been a philosophy, a set of ideas to hold, insists instead on water over a body and bread in a mouth, and refuses to let you be a Christian only in your head. The answer runs down to how God made the world and how he saved it. He made matter and called it good, very good, and when the world went wrong he did not rescue souls out of bodies but took on a body himself, the Word made flesh. Bell takes the strong case for the ordinance instinct, that grace comes through faith in Christ and not through a ritual worked mechanically, and grants it fully. Then he takes the strong case for the sacrament instinct, that God is generous enough to meet his people in the ordinary stuff of a creation he loves, and grants that too. He lands, as a Baptist, cautious in his words and large in his wonder, unwilling to call the sign empty and unwilling to make it magic, and he names the whole difference a matter among brothers and sisters, not a line between the saved and the lost. The water and the table are not the boring part left over from an older religion. They are God taking the world he made seriously enough to save us through it.

keyScripture.why: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth, naming the hinge on which the whole logic of the sacraments turns, that the God who could have stayed invisible took on matter, so a faith with an incarnation at its center cannot despise the physical things through which he chooses to reach us.

discussion.q: Bell says he arrived at faith assuming the real world is only what you can measure and that anything holy must be invisible and private. Before tonight, did you quietly think of the water and the bread as leftover ritual, the optional part of a faith that is really about believing the right things?
discussion.behind: Surface the modern instinct before naming anything against it. Most people in the room absorbed, without ever choosing it, the assumption that spirituality is inward and matter is just matter. The point is not to shame it but to expose it, because you cannot see why God uses physical signs until you have noticed the reason you assumed he would not. Land it on honesty about the assumption, not on the right answer yet.

discussion.q: Scripture does not open with God tolerating matter as a regrettable necessity. It opens with God making a physical world and calling it good, and very good. What changes about the water and the bread when you start from a creation God delights in rather than a world he is trying to get us out of?
discussion.behind: Move the room from a rescue-from-the-body picture to a redemption-of-the-body one. Much popular Christianity smuggles in an old heresy, that the material is low and the spiritual is high and salvation means escape. Help them feel that the sacraments only make sense inside a faith that says God made stuff, loves stuff, and saves through stuff, because he is not embarrassed by the world he made.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for calling these signs ordinances, practices the Lord commanded that we obey and proclaim, careful never to say the water or the bread carries a power of its own. What is true in that caution that you would not want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the first session, and honor the free-church people in the room. The ordinance instinct is guarding something real, that no one is saved by getting wet or by eating, that grace comes through faith in Christ. Make sure no one hears the sacramental language as if the ritual works mechanically. The caution is a genuine biblical loyalty, not a lesser faith.

discussion.q: Augustine called a sacrament a visible word, the gospel made touchable, reaching you through the eye and the hand and the tongue rather than only the ear. Where in your life has a truth you could hold at arm's length as an idea gotten past your defenses only when it got onto your body?
discussion.behind: This is the experiential center. The sermon reaches the mind; the sign reaches the whole person. Draw out real moments, the meal that meant more than the words, the physical act that made a belief suddenly weighty. The aim is to feel why God does not only tell his people they belong but washes them and feeds them, because we come to know things with our hands.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he spent years more comfortable with a well-made argument than with a wet head or a shared cup, because the argument he controlled and the sign he could only receive. Where have you preferred to keep your faith in your head, where you are in charge of it?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication, including the leader. The preference for the idea over the sign is often a preference for control, for a faith we manage rather than one we receive with open hands. Go first if the room is slow. Name your own habit of trusting the thing you can argue over the thing you can only be given.

objections.objection: The physical signs are just religious theater. What matters is the state of your heart before God, and pouring water or eating bread cannot change anything real. Insisting on the rituals is exactly the empty externalism Jesus attacked in the Pharisees.
objections.response: Grant the real danger first, because it is a danger Scripture itself names. A ritual performed while the heart is far off is precisely what the prophets and Jesus condemned, and no one is saved by the water or the bread apart from faith in Christ. If the objection is guarding against a religion of mere external motions, it is guarding something true and worth guarding. But notice the false step underneath, the assumption that the physical and the heartfelt are opposites, that if a thing is bodily it must be empty. Christianity denies exactly that. The God who made a good material world and then took on flesh does not treat the body as the enemy of the heart. He reaches the heart through the body on purpose. The sign is not a substitute for faith. It is faith given something to touch, the gospel handed to a creature who was made to know with hands and not only with a mind, and to call that theater is to miss why God became flesh in the first place.

objections.objection: You can call it a sacrament or an ordinance, but the two traditions clearly mean different things, and one of them has to be wrong. Papering over a real theological disagreement to keep everyone comfortable is dishonest.
objections.response: Honor the demand for honesty, because it is right that the words carry different weight and the difference is not nothing. The sacramental traditions mean that God actually does something through the sign, a means of grace and not only a picture, and the ordinance traditions mean a commanded act of obedience and proclamation, careful never to locate a power in the elements themselves. Those are not identical, and this study will not pretend they are. But hear the distinction that keeps it from being a war. The disagreement is about how much God does through a sign both sides receive from him in faith, not about whether Christ saves by grace, which both confess, and not about who belongs to him. It is possible to hold your own position with conviction, to think the other side has gone slightly too far or not far enough, and still to recognize a brother, because the line the New Testament draws around the people of God is faith in the crucified and risen Christ, and it runs straight through both traditions rather than between them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you kept your faith safely in your head, a set of ideas you could hold and control, and quietly avoided the signs that ask you to receive something with your body and your hands?
sessions.practice: This week, the next time you take communion or watch a baptism, do not treat it as the part of the service to get through. Slow down inside it. Feel the water or the bread as the gospel made touchable, God reaching a creature with a body through the good stuff of the world he made. Afterward, write down what you noticed when you stopped treating the sign as a formality and let it preach to you the way a sermon does.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made a material world and called it good, and when we ruined it you did not rescue us out of our bodies but took one on, the Word made flesh, hands and scars and all. Forgive us for treating your signs as leftover religion, for preferring the ideas we can argue over the gifts we can only receive. Teach us that you are not embarrassed by the world you made, that you meet us in water and bread because we are the creatures you formed from dust and love. Get past our defenses through our very hands. Make the water and the table preach to us what our proud minds keep holding at a distance. Amen.
reflection: Where did I absorb the assumption that the real world is only what I can measure and that anything holy must be invisible, and what has that quietly done to how I treat the sacraments?
Do I actually believe God is generous enough to meet me in ordinary water and bread, or do I secretly think the physical is beneath him?
What would change in my faith if I let the signs reach me the way the incarnation reached the world, through the body and not only the mind?
sessions.teaching: A man sat in Bell's study who had followed Jesus for a decade and had never once been baptized, and when Bell asked him why, the man said, with no defensiveness at all, that he did not really see the point of getting wet. His faith, he explained, was inward. It was a matter of the heart and the mind, of what he believed and how he lived, and the water and the bread struck him as leftover religion, ritual for people who needed props to feel something. Bell says he did not argue, because he understood the instinct completely. He came to faith from atheism, and he arrived carrying the exact conviction the whole modern world carries in its bones, that the real world is the world you can weigh and measure, and that if there is a spiritual world at all it is invisible and private, happening somewhere behind the eyes where no one else can check. So we begin here, because this instinct is not a small or foolish thing. It is the water the entire culture swims in, the quiet assumption that matter is just matter, inert stuff, and that anything holy must therefore be immaterial. And the strange, stubborn fact is that Christianity refuses it. The faith that could so easily have been a philosophy, a tidy set of ideas to affirm, insists instead on water poured over a body and bread broken in a mouth. It will not let you be a Christian only in your head. The real question is why. Why does this faith, more than almost any other, drag the holy down into the physical and keep it there. The answer runs all the way down to how God made the world and how he chose to save it. Genesis does not open with God grudgingly tolerating matter as a necessary evil. It opens with God making a physical world on purpose and calling it good, and then, when it is finished, very good. The stuff is not the problem. The stuff is his idea. And then, when the world went wrong, watch what God did not do. He did not rescue us by extracting our souls from our bodies and carrying them off somewhere cleaner and more spiritual. He did the opposite. He took on a body. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and this is the hinge on which everything turns. The incarnation means the eternal God has hands now. He ate broiled fish after the resurrection. He keeps his scars. A faith with an incarnation at its center cannot despise matter, because God himself wore it. Athanasius saw this clearly in the fourth century, that he became man so that we might be made divine, and the whole rescue only works if the flesh is not the thing to escape but the very thing God takes up in order to heal it. Once you have seen that, the signs stop being strange. Augustine gave the church a phrase that has held for sixteen centuries, that a sacrament is a visible word, a sign of a sacred thing, an invisible grace given a form you can see and touch. The sermon reaches you through the ear. The sign reaches you through the eye and the hand and the tongue, the gospel made touchable, so that a truth you could hold at arm's length as an idea gets past your defenses by getting onto your body. Now the disagreement, and we take it up honestly and early because it will run quietly under all five weeks. Christians divide on what to call these signs and on how much they actually do. Some traditions, the Catholic, the Orthodox, the Lutheran, the Reformed, use the word sacrament, and they mean that God genuinely does something through the sign, that it is a means of grace and not only a picture. Others, many Baptists and free-church evangelicals, prefer the word ordinance, meaning a practice the Lord himself ordained and commanded, an act of obedience and public proclamation, and they are careful never to say the water or the bread carries a power of its own. Take the strong case for each, because both are guarding something precious. The ordinance instinct is protecting the truth that no one is saved by getting wet or by eating, that grace comes through faith in the crucified Christ and not through a ritual worked like a machine. The sacrament instinct is protecting the equally precious truth that God is generous enough to meet his people in the ordinary matter of a creation he called good, that he does not only speak to us but stoops to feed us. Here is where I stand, and I will name it as this study asks everyone to name it. I am a Baptist pastor, and I find myself cautious in my words, closer to ordinance, and large in my wonder, closer to sacrament, unwilling to call the sign an empty picture and equally unwilling to make it magic. And I confess I spent years treating these signs as the boring part of the service, more comfortable in a pulpit with a well-made argument than with a wet head or a shared cup, because the argument I controlled and the sign I could only receive. James K. A. Smith has pressed the modern church hard on exactly this, that we imagine ourselves brains on sticks, formed by ideas, when in truth we are formed far more by what our bodies do, by practice and habit and repetition. The sacraments know this about us. God does not hand his people a doctrine of belonging and leave it on the page. He washes them, and he feeds them, because he made us creatures who come to know things with our hands. The water and the table are not the leftover religion. They are God taking the goodness of the world he made seriously enough to save us through it.

scriptureStudy.note: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. The material world is not a mistake God is working around. It is his deliberate work, pronounced good, which is the first reason the faith is unafraid to locate the holy in water and bread.

And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The incarnation is the ground of every sacrament. The God who took on a body cannot despise the physical things through which he chooses to reach us, because he made himself one of them.

They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them. The risen Christ eats. The resurrection is not the shedding of a body but the raising of one, which tells you what God thinks of matter even at the end of the story.

For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. Paul refuses every attempt to treat the created and physical as beneath the spiritual, a refusal that lands directly on how we regard the elements.

We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death. Paul does not speak of baptism as a bare symbol standing off to the side. He speaks as if the sign and the reality it signifies are joined, which is the very tension the two traditions handle differently.

The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Paul uses the language of participation for the bread and the cup, refusing to reduce the meal to a memory, which is why the debate over the table is worth taking seriously.

For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. The fullness of God dwells in a body. A faith that confesses this cannot consistently treat bodily signs as unspiritual, because its God is embodied at the center.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session only gestures at, because the instinct that matter is low and spirit is high did not come from Scripture and the church had to fight it early. In the second century the various movements later grouped under the name Gnostic taught that the material world was the botched work of a lesser god and that salvation meant the escape of the spirit from the prison of the body, and Irenaeus of Lyon answered them near the year 180 by insisting that the same God made the flesh and redeemed it, and that the eucharist itself proves the point, because bread and wine from the created earth become the vehicle of grace. A group can weigh how persistently this old error keeps returning in new clothes, in every version of Christianity that treats the body as an embarrassment and heaven as a disembodied escape rather than as resurrection and new creation. Set that against Augustine, who near the year 400 gave the West its lasting grammar for the signs, the sacrament as a visible word, a sign that both points to and, in the traditions that follow him most closely, conveys the grace it signifies. Then take the contemporary turn with James K. A. Smith, whose work on Christian formation argues that human beings are not primarily thinking things but desiring, embodied, habit-formed things, so that what shapes us most deeply is not the ideas we consent to but the practices our bodies repeat. A group should test this against Scripture rather than swallowing it whole, granting that the mind matters and the truth must be believed, while noticing how exactly it names why God gave his people not only a message to affirm but water to be washed in and a table to return to again and again. The aim is not to make the sacraments the whole of the faith, which they are not, but to recover why a God who made a good world and took on flesh would refuse to save embodied creatures by information alone.
sessions.caseStudy: A member of your group is a lifelong, serious Christian who reads widely and prizes sound doctrine, and when the conversation turns to the physical signs he grows visibly impatient, saying the real substance of the faith is the truth we believe and that all this attention to water and bread feels like a distraction from the gospel itself. He is not cynical, and he loves the Scriptures, and his instinct to guard the centrality of the gospel is genuinely good. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it presses him. He is right that the signs are not a substitute for faith and that no ritual saves apart from Christ, and you should say so plainly and mean it. But notice what his impatience may be costing, because the God who gave him the truth to believe also gave him a body and gave that body water and a table, and to treat the signs as a distraction from the gospel is to be more spiritual than the incarnation, which located the fullness of God in flesh. Do not let him win the point by opposing the sign to the truth, as though they were rivals. Honor his love for the gospel fully, and still ask him, gently, why the God who could have saved us by pure instruction chose instead to wash us and feed us, and what that choice says about the kind of creatures we are and the kind of God he is.
