sessions.title: The Table That Makes Us One
sessions.aim: To read 1 Corinthians 11 the way Paul wrote it, as a rebuke of a church that turned the Lord's Supper into a display of its own divisions, to recover self-examination as honesty about how we treat the body rather than morbid introspection, and to see the table as the proclamation of the Lord's death and the sign of a unity we are called to live and not only to receive.
sessions.summary: Bell says the passage most churches read at communion, the solemn warning about examining yourself lest you eat and drink judgment, has been so wrenched from its setting that it now produces the exact opposite of what Paul intended, a table of anxious, isolated individuals each searching their own heart for hidden sin, when Paul wrote it to rebuke a church that was humiliating its poor members at the very meal meant to make them one. The real question is what Paul was actually angry about, and the answer is not private impurity but public division. In Corinth the wealthy arrived early and ate their fill while the poor, who could not leave work, arrived to nothing, so that the Lord's Supper had become a display of the very class divisions the gospel abolishes. That, Paul says, is why you eat and drink judgment, because you do not discern the body, and the body he means is not only the bread but the church. Bell takes the strong case for the introspective reading, that self-examination and taking the table worthily are genuinely biblical and guard against a casual, presumptuous approach to holy things. He grants it fully. But he insists the examination Paul commands is first horizontal before it is vertical, an honest look at how you are treating your brothers and sisters, and only a church deaf to its own divisions could read this passage as a call to private soul-searching and miss that it is about how the rich treated the poor. Then the reversal and the self-implication. We have taken the one meal that proclaims a death that reconciles enemies and made it, too often, a marker of who is respectable enough to belong. The table proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, and a church that eats it while despising part of its own body proclaims a lie. The meal was meant to make us one. It still can. It still judges the church that refuses to let it.

keyScripture.why: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes, naming the Supper as a proclamation, a preached gospel enacted with the body, so that a church divided against itself at the table proclaims a death that reconciles while living a division that denies it.

discussion.q: Bell says the examine yourself passage has been so pulled from its setting that it now produces the opposite of what Paul intended, anxious individuals searching for private sin. When you have heard those words at communion, what did you think Paul was warning you about?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the inherited misreading, gently, because almost everyone has received this passage as a call to morbid introspection. Draw out the anxiety it has produced, the fear of taking the table wrongly, the private hunt for hidden sin. The aim is to expose the assumption before restoring Paul's actual concern, which is corporate and not merely individual.

discussion.q: Paul was not angry about private impurity but about public division, that the rich in Corinth ate their fill while the poor got nothing at the very meal meant to make them one. Why does it matter that the sin he condemns is how they treated each other, not what was hidden in their hearts?
discussion.behind: Press on the horizontal reading, the heart of the session. Paul's rebuke is about a church humiliating its poor at the table. Help the room feel how much changes when discerning the body means recognizing the church, not just reverencing the bread. It moves examination from a private mirror to an honest look at how we treat one another.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that self-examination and taking the table worthily are genuinely biblical and guard against a casual approach to holy things. What is true in that, and how does it fit with Paul's concern being mainly about division?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves so the corrective does not overcorrect. Examination is real and biblical, and reverence at the table matters. The point is not to abolish self-examination but to reorient it, to see that the worthiness Paul demands is first about how you are treating the body of Christ. Let the vertical and horizontal hold together rather than replacing one with the other.

discussion.q: Bell says the table proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, and a church that eats it while despising part of its own body proclaims a lie. Where does the way your church, or you, come to the table quietly contradict the reconciliation the meal proclaims?
discussion.behind: Move toward self-implication. The table preaches a death that reconciles enemies, and a divided church eating it preaches against its own message. Invite honesty about the divisions carried right up to the table, class, race, old grudges, the person avoided in the parking lot and passed the bread an hour later. Keep it about our own church, not others.

discussion.q: Bell says the meal was meant to make us one and still judges the church that refuses to let it. If the Lord's table is the rehearsal of a reconciled people, what would have to change in how you come to it, and who you come to it beside?
discussion.behind: Close on the constructive turn and the weight. The table is not only a critique of division but the ongoing means of a unity the church is called to live. Ask what repentance and reconciliation the table calls for before the next time they eat it. End in weight rather than tidy resolution, the meal still judging and still healing the church willing to be made one.

objections.objection: The passage clearly says to examine yourself before taking communion, so it obviously is about personal sin and coming to the table with a clean heart. Making it about social divisions is just reading modern politics back into Paul.
objections.response: Grant that the call to examine yourself is genuinely there and genuinely means examine yourself, so this is not about deleting personal responsibility or turning Paul into a social program. Reverence and honesty before a holy table are real biblical demands. But read the whole chapter and notice what Paul is examining them about, because he tells you plainly. He is furious that when they come together it is not for the better but for the worse, that there are divisions among them, that one goes hungry while another gets drunk, that they humiliate those who have nothing. That is the context of examine yourself, and the body they fail to discern is, Paul has just spent chapters arguing, the church, the many members who are one body in Christ. So this is not modern politics read backward. It is Paul's own argument read forward. The self-examination he commands is first an honest look at how you are treating the brothers and sisters you eat beside, and only a church already deaf to its own divisions could hear this passage as a summons to private introspection and miss that it was written because the rich were shaming the poor at the Lord's own table.

objections.objection: If you make the table about unity and welcome, you will end up letting anyone take communion regardless of how they live, which cheapens the whole thing. Some fencing of the table is necessary to keep it holy.
objections.response: Take the concern seriously, because it is not wrong that the table is holy and that Scripture does warn against eating it carelessly, and a church that treats communion as a casual snack for anyone in any condition has lost something Paul would rebuke. There is a right fencing of the table, a call to come in faith and repentance, and this study does not deny it. But watch the direction the fence tends to run, because in Corinth the problem was not that the table was too open but that it was effectively closed to the poor, guarded by the comfortable against the very people Christ died to include. The danger Paul names is not lax welcome but proud exclusion, a church using the meal to mark who is respectable enough to belong. So fence the table where Scripture fences it, at faith and repentance, and refuse to fence it where the Corinthians did, at wealth and class and respectability and every human division the cross abolished. A holy table is one where sinners come humbly to a gracious host, not one where the settled decide who is good enough for grace.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the person you carry a division with, a grudge or a coldness or a quiet contempt, whom you will pass the bread beside and call it communion, and what would it mean to be reconciled before you eat?
sessions.practice: This week, before you take communion, do the examination Paul actually commands. Look not only inward at your private sins but outward at how you are treating the body of Christ, the brother you have written off, the person at church you avoid, the division you have made peace with. Then, if you are able, go and be reconciled before you eat, or at least name the division to God and take one step toward mending it. Write down what it costs you to let the table judge not only your heart but your relationships, and what it might heal.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you gave your body and your blood to reconcile enemies to God and to one another, and you left your church a meal to proclaim that reconciliation until you come, and we confess we have too often eaten it while despising part of your body. Forgive us for turning a table of grace into a marker of who is respectable enough to belong, for the divisions we carry right up to the bread. Give us the honest examination Paul commands, not only the private mirror but the harder look at how we treat one another. Make us one at your table, so that when we proclaim your death we are not proclaiming a lie. Reconcile us before we eat, and by this meal keep making your divided people the one body you died to gather. Amen.
reflection: Have I read the examine yourself passage as a call to private soul-searching and missed that Paul wrote it about how the church was treating its poor?
What divisions do I carry right up to the table, and how does my church quietly contradict the reconciliation the meal proclaims?
If the Lord's table is the rehearsal of a reconciled people, who would I need to be reconciled to before I honestly eat it again?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the passage most churches solemnly read every time they take communion, the warning about examining yourself so that you do not eat and drink judgment on yourself, has been so thoroughly wrenched out of its setting that it now produces the precise opposite of what Paul intended. In most churches it produces a table of anxious, isolated individuals, heads bowed, each one searching their own heart for some hidden sin that might make it dangerous to take the bread, wondering if they are worthy, hoping they have not missed anything. And Paul wrote those words in a white heat of anger at a church that was humiliating its poor members at the very meal that was supposed to make them one. So we have to read the chapter the way Paul wrote it, because the misreading is not harmless. It has turned a rebuke of division into a summons to introspection, and in doing so it has let the church commit the exact sin Paul was condemning while feeling solemn about it. Here is what was actually happening in Corinth. The Lord's Supper in the early church was a real meal, and in Corinth the wealthy members, who had the leisure, arrived early and ate and drank their fill, while the poor members, the laborers and the slaves who could not leave work until later, arrived to find the food gone and the wine drunk. So the meal that proclaimed a Lord who emptied himself for the lowly had become a weekly display of the very class divisions the gospel exists to abolish, the rich full and the poor shamed, at the table of the crucified. And that, Paul says, is why you eat and drink judgment on yourselves, because you do not discern the body. Now hold onto that phrase, the body, because everything turns on it. For most of my life I heard discern the body as a command to reverence the bread, to recognize that the elements are holy and to take them with due gravity. But Paul has just spent the previous chapters of this letter developing one great image, that the church is a body, many members, Jew and Greek, slave and free, the weaker parts indispensable, the whole thing one in Christ. The body they were failing to discern was not only the bread. It was one another. They were despising the church of God and humiliating those who had nothing, and they could not see it, because they had learned to take the table without ever looking honestly at how they were treating the people they took it beside. Take the strong case for the introspective reading first, because there is real truth in it and I do not want to overcorrect into nonsense. Self-examination is genuinely biblical. Coming to the table worthily is a real command, and a casual, presumptuous, careless approach to the holy things of God is a real danger that Scripture warns against more than once. Reverence matters. Honesty before God matters. Grant all of it. But the examination Paul commands here is first horizontal before it is vertical. Before it sends you inward to hunt for private sin, it sends you outward to ask how you are treating your brothers and sisters, whether the way you come to this table honors or humiliates the body of Christ. And only a church already deaf to its own divisions could read this passage, written because the rich were starving the poor at communion, and come away thinking it is mostly about whether you had an impure thought on the drive over. Now the reversal, and I stand inside it with everyone else. We have taken the one meal in all the world that proclaims a death that reconciles enemies, that tears down the wall between Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, and we have made it, too often, a quiet marker of who is respectable enough to belong. I have passed the bread to a person I was cold toward and called it communion. I have led a table while carrying a division in my own chest that the meal in my hands was preaching against. Paul says that as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. The table is a sermon preached with the body, a proclamation. And a church that eats it while despising part of its own body is proclaiming a lie, announcing a reconciliation it refuses to live. So the examination the table demands is not finally the morbid search for private failure that has made so many Christians afraid of the bread. It is the harder, humbler question of whether you are one with the body you are about to eat with, whether there is a brother to be reconciled to before you come, whether the division you have made your peace with is being carried right up to the table of the Lord who died to end it. The meal was given to make us one. It still can. And it still judges the church that refuses to let it. Come to it, then, not mainly to search your own heart in isolation, but to be made one with the body of Christ, and where you cannot come in peace with a brother, go and be reconciled first, and then come, and eat, and proclaim with your body a death that actually brings enemies home.

scriptureStudy.note: When you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. Paul names the problem at the outset, and it is division, not private impurity, which sets the meaning of everything he says about the table that follows.

One goes hungry, another gets drunk. Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? The specific sin is the rich shaming the poor at the meal, the concrete context of the warning about eating unworthily.

Whoever eats in an unworthy manner will be guilty, for anyone who eats without discerning the body eats judgment on himself. Discerning the body means recognizing the church, the many members Paul has been describing, not only reverencing the bread.

Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread. The one loaf is itself an argument for unity, the shared meal making and signifying one body, which is why division at the table is a contradiction in terms.

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. Paul's whole body theology stands behind chapter 11, so the divisions of wealth and status at the table deny the baptism that made them one.

First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Jesus commands reconciliation before worship, the very order Paul presses at the table, honesty about how we treat one another before we approach the holy things.

For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility. The cross the table proclaims is the death that reconciles enemies, which is why a divided church at the table proclaims against its own gospel.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the setting Paul wrote into, because the social world of Corinth explains the abuse and sharpens the warning. New Testament scholars such as Gordon Fee have shown that the earliest Lord's Supper was joined to a real communal meal, often held in the home of a wealthier member whose dining room seated only a few while the rest crowded a larger courtyard, so that the physical architecture of the Roman house reinforced the very class distinctions the gospel abolished, the honored few reclining with the host and the many left outside. Roman society was ordered by patronage and rank to a degree the modern reader struggles to feel, and for the church to reproduce that ranking at the table of a crucified Lord was not a minor lapse but a denial of the cross enacted in the seating chart. A group can weigh how exactly this names a temptation the church has never outgrown, the quiet sorting of people by wealth and status and respectability carried right into the room where we proclaim that Christ died for all of them equally. Set this beside the theme of proclamation, that the Supper preaches, that as often as we eat it we announce the Lord's death, and press the hard question the session builds toward. If the table is a sermon preached with the body, then the unity or division of the church at the table is part of the message it preaches, so that a segregated or stratified or grudge-bearing communion proclaims a false gospel however true the words spoken over the bread. A group should ask honestly where their own church, and their own heart, carries division to the table, whether of class or race or old wounds, and should recover the meal not only as comfort but as the ongoing judgment and healing of a people being made one. The aim is to let the table examine the church as Paul meant it to, and to send people not to a private mirror but to a brother, to be reconciled before they eat.
sessions.caseStudy: A member of your group is diligent and sincere and has quietly stopped taking communion for months, and when the session reaches the examine yourself passage she admits, with real distress, that she never feels worthy enough, that she is always sure there is some sin she has not adequately confessed, and that the warning about eating judgment has made the table a source of dread rather than grace. She is not being dramatic. She has been handed a misreading and it has wounded a tender conscience. Here is the work for the leader, and it must bring genuine relief without becoming careless. Do not simply tell her worthiness does not matter, because Paul does say examine yourself and a flippant reassurance would ring false to her honesty. Instead give her the passage back whole. Show her that the unworthy manner Paul condemns was not a tender conscience with unconfessed sin but the proud rich humiliating the poor, that the worthiness he calls for is not moral perfection but coming honestly as a sinner to a gracious host, discerning and loving the body rather than despising it. Help her see that the table was never meant to be a test she passes but a meal she is fed at, and that a heart afraid it is not good enough is exactly the heart the crucified host spread the table for. Send her back to the bread, not away from it, with the dread replaced by the welcome Paul actually intended.

leaderPrimer: The particular danger of a study on the sacraments is that it can turn into a debate club. You are handling the two subjects, baptism and the Lord's Supper, over which the church has argued longest and most bitterly, and if you let it, the room will divide into teams and spend five weeks scoring points, the Baptist against the Presbyterian, the memorialist against the one who believes in real presence, everyone defending the tradition they happened to be raised in and no one being formed. So set the rule the first night and hold it every night after. The goal of this study is not to win the argument. It is to understand what these signs are, to hold real convictions with real humility, and to state the position you disagree with so well that its own defenders would sign your summary. Make people articulate the view they do not hold, in its strongest form, before they are allowed to critique it. That single discipline will do more for the room than any lecture. Be clear, and be repetitive, about the difference between what the faith stands or falls on and what faithful churches disagree on and remain one. The deity and resurrection of Christ, salvation by grace through the cross, these are first-order and not up for a vote. The timing of baptism and the metaphysics of the Supper are second-order, worth studying and deciding and holding, never worth breaking fellowship over. The writer is a Baptist and says so plainly, and he still labors to state the paedobaptist case and the range of communion views at their strongest, and he expects the leader to do the same, whatever the leader's own tradition. If your group is drawn from one tradition, work extra hard to represent the others fairly, because a room that only ever hears the other side caricatured will leave more tribal than it came. If your group is mixed, you have a gift, and your job is to keep the temperature low and the depth high, to let people disagree and stay brothers. Watch for two kinds of people who need care. There is the new believer who has never been baptized or has never understood the table, for whom this study is an invitation, not a debate, and you should make sure the arguing does not drown out the wonder. And there is the person with a wounded conscience, especially around the examine yourself passage, who has been made afraid of the table, and who needs the passage given back whole rather than another warning laid on. The writer does not lead this from above it. He is a pastor still learning to hold his own convictions with more love than he used to, who has enjoyed winning these arguments more than he enjoyed the brother across the table. Go in the same way, as someone still being taught by the water and the meal, and the room will follow you into honesty instead of into teams.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell me my baptism was wrong, or that my church has communion wrong?
faq.a: No. The whole method of the study is to state each position, on baptism and on the Lord's Supper, in its strongest form, the form its own best defenders would recognize, before any verdict is named. The writer is a Baptist and says so plainly, and he still works to make the infant-baptism case and the range of communion views as strong as their own advocates would want them made. The point is not to declare your tradition wrong but to help you understand what the sacraments are, to hold your convictions with more depth and more humility, and to see that these are second-order questions on which faithful, Christ-loving churches have disagreed for centuries while remaining one body. You will likely finish more settled in your own convictions and far more able to honor a brother who holds another.

faq.q: Why does the study keep calling baptism and communion second-order issues? Do they not matter?
faq.a: They matter a great deal, and the study takes them seriously enough to spend five sessions on them. Second-order does not mean unimportant. It means they are not the doctrines the Christian faith stands or falls on, the way the deity and bodily resurrection of Christ, or salvation by grace through the cross, are first-order and non-negotiable. Baptism and the Supper are worth studying, worth deciding, worth holding with real conviction. They are not worth breaking fellowship over, because faithful churches have landed on opposite sides of them for five hundred years while confessing the same Lord. The study asks you to hold the difference between what the creeds bind and what divides faithful churches but not the faith, and to give your convictions the weight they deserve without turning them into tests of who belongs to Christ.

faq.q: What is the difference between a sacrament and an ordinance?
faq.a: The words mark a real difference in emphasis between traditions. The sacramental traditions, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed, use the word sacrament and mean that God actually does something through the sign, that it is a means of grace and not only a picture. The free-church traditions, many Baptists and evangelicals, prefer the word ordinance, meaning a practice the Lord himself ordained and commanded, an act of obedience and public proclamation, careful never to locate a saving power in the water or the bread themselves. The study takes both seriously. The ordinance instinct guards the truth that no one is saved by getting wet or by eating, that grace comes through faith in Christ. The sacramental instinct guards the truth that God is generous enough to meet his people in the ordinary matter of a creation he called good. The writer lands cautious in his words and large in his wonder, and treats the difference as one among brothers and sisters, not a line between the saved and the lost.

faq.q: Does the study say what happens at communion, or does it dodge the question?
faq.a: It does not dodge it. Session four states four serious views at their strongest, the memorial view associated with Zwingli, the spiritual-presence view associated with Calvin, the sacramental-union view associated with Luther, and transubstantiation as defined by the Roman Catholic Church, and it names the biblical and pastoral instinct each one is guarding. Then the writer names where he lands, as a Baptist who cannot rest in bare memory, closer to Calvin, confessing a real spiritual presence at a table where the living Christ genuinely meets and feeds his people by his Spirit. He holds it as a second-order conviction, states the objections he has not fully answered, and insists that the tragedy of the table is not that Christians have understood it differently but that they have made a meal of grace into a border checkpoint. The study takes a position and refuses to make it a wall.

faq.q: I am not sure I even believe all this. Can a skeptic get anything out of this study?
faq.a: Yes, and the study is written with you partly in mind. It does not begin by demanding you accept the signs. It begins by taking seriously the very instinct you may be bringing, that the real world is what you can measure and that religious rituals look like leftover superstition. The writer came to faith from atheism carrying exactly that instinct, and he does not pretend it away. What the study offers is an honest account of why Christianity, unlike a mere philosophy, refuses to stay in the head and insists on things you can touch, and how that refusal is rooted in a God who made a material world and called it good and then took on a body himself. You do not have to share the conclusion to find the reasoning worth following, or to notice that a faith willing to argue this hard and this long about the meaning of water and bread is treating the physical world with more seriousness, not less, than the skeptic expected.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session on Romans 6 and identity instead of just explaining baptism?
faq.a: Because the argument over who gets baptized, for all its importance, can distract the church from what baptism actually declares, which both traditions confess together and confess with awe. Session three sets the debate down and stands where every tradition stands, in Paul's teaching that baptism is a burial, a union with Christ in his death and resurrection, the burial of an old identity and the raising of a new one. This is not abstract. It speaks directly to the person weighed down by shame, defined by a past failure or an old sin, because baptism declares over them an identity truer than their history, a death they did not perform and a resurrection they did not earn. The session distinguishes a change of status, which is complete in Christ, from a change of condition, the slow remaking of habits across a lifetime, and shows that the Christian life is not becoming new by trying harder but learning to live from a newness already given. It is the most personally useful session for anyone fighting to believe they are not what they were.

faq.q: Is the study just going to make me anxious about taking communion the wrong way?
faq.a: It does the opposite, and session five is built to undo exactly that anxiety. The passage about examining yourself lest you eat and drink judgment has been so pulled from its setting that it now produces fear, individuals searching their hearts for some hidden sin that might make the table dangerous. But Paul wrote those words to rebuke a church where the rich were eating their fill while the poor went hungry at the very meal meant to make them one. The sin he condemns is not private impurity but public division, and the body they failed to discern was the church, not only the bread. So the examination Paul commands is first an honest look at how you are treating your brothers and sisters. The study gives the passage back whole, replacing the dread with the welcome Paul actually intended, and it is especially careful with the wounded conscience who has stopped coming to the table out of fear, sending that person back to the bread rather than away from it.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I am not a theologian and do not know all the views myself?
faq.a: That is exactly whom the study was written for. Every session carries the teaching in full, states each contested position in its strongest form so you do not have to construct the arguments yourself, and puts the answer behind every discussion question. The four views of communion and the two of baptism are laid out plainly, with the biblical texts each one leans on, so a volunteer with no seminary training can represent them fairly. Your real job is not to be an expert but to keep the room honest and humble, to make people state the view they disagree with well before they critique it, and to hold the line between first-order and second-order matters. Read the leader primer, walk through the teaching before your group meets, and lead not as the one with all the answers but as someone learning alongside the room what these signs actually are.

faq.q: My group is all from one tradition. Is this study still worth doing?
faq.a: Yes, and in some ways the discipline matters more for a single-tradition group, because a room that only ever hears the other positions caricatured will leave more tribal than it arrived. The study is designed to make you state the views you do not hold in their strongest form, which is precisely the muscle a homogeneous group tends not to build. You will come away more settled in your own convictions, better able to say why you hold them, and far more able to recognize as a genuine brother the Christian down the road who baptizes differently or understands the table differently. If anything, a group that shares a tradition should work extra hard at the steelman, and the leader should feel free to argue the other side vigorously so that no one leaves thinking the people who disagree with them are simply careless with the Bible.

faq.q: Does taking a clear position, as the writer does, contradict the call to be irenic?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful to model that it does not. Being irenic does not mean having no convictions or pretending every view is equally right. It means holding your convictions with courage and with love, stating the other side fairly, and refusing to make a second-order disagreement a test of fellowship. The writer names where he lands on both baptism and the Supper, plainly and without hedging, and he also names the strongest objections he has not fully answered and insists that those who disagree are brothers he expects to spend eternity beside. That is the pattern the study teaches, conviction and humility in the same hand. The failure is not in having a position. The failure is in being unable to state the other view honestly, or in turning a matter Scripture leaves genuinely contested into a wall Christ never built.

faq.q: Why does the writer keep implicating himself instead of just teaching the doctrine?
faq.a: Because the method is part of the message. The writer does not stand above these subjects as a neutral expert. He confesses that he spent years treating the sacraments as the boring part of the service, that he has been sharper in the baptism argument than love allowed, that he has guarded the Lord's table more fiercely than he has loved the ones on the other side of it, that he has carried divisions right up to a meal that preaches against them. He does this on purpose, because a study on the sacraments could so easily become a way to feel superior to the traditions that get it wrong, and self-implication is the antidote. You cannot repent of a thing you are busy congratulating yourself for getting right, and you cannot call a room to humility about these disputes from a height. By standing inside the failures he describes, the writer makes it possible for the people actually in the room to be formed rather than merely armed.

faq.q: What if someone in the group has never been baptized or has never really understood communion?
faq.a: That is one of the best reasons to do the study, and the leader should make sure the arguing never drowns out the invitation. For a new believer, or for someone who has drifted from these signs, the study is not first a debate but a door. Session one recovers why the signs matter at all, session two calls the unbaptized believer to the sign at the door and says plainly it is not meant to be skipped, session three shows what baptism declares about who they now are, and sessions four and five open the table as a meal of grace and unity rather than a test to fear. If someone in your group professes faith in Christ and has never been baptized, take it seriously and connect them to your pastor, because the study treats baptism as the God-appointed sign of belonging, not an optional extra. Keep the wonder in the room, not only the argument.

timeline.event: On the night he is betrayed, Jesus takes bread and the cup with his disciples and institutes the meal, saying this is my body and this is my blood of the covenant, and after his resurrection commands his church to baptize the nations, giving the two signs that will mark his people for two thousand years.

At Pentecost Peter preaches repent and be baptized, and about three thousand are baptized in a single day, establishing baptism as the sign received at entrance into the church and beginning the pattern the New Testament records of preaching, faith, and baptism.

Paul writes to the Corinthians the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper we possess, rebuking a church that shamed its poor at the table and teaching that to eat without discerning the body is to eat judgment, and that the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.

The Didache, an early church manual, gives practical instructions for baptism, preferring running water and describing the baptism of those first taught, and for the thanksgiving meal, the earliest window we have into how the young church practiced the two signs.

Justin Martyr, defending the faith to a pagan emperor, describes the baptism of new believers and the weekly gathering at which bread and a cup of wine and water are shared, one of the fullest early accounts of Christian worship and the sacraments.

Cyprian and a council of North African bishops debate not whether to baptize infants but whether to wait until the eighth day in imitation of circumcision, concluding they need not, evidence that infant baptism was by then an established and widespread practice.

Augustine gives the Western church its lasting definition of a sacrament as a visible word, a sign of a sacred thing, and defends infant baptism against the Pelagians, shaping the theology of the signs for more than a thousand years, for both better and worse.

The Fourth Lateran Council uses the word transubstantiation to describe the change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, giving official form to a doctrine of the Supper that the Reformation will later contest.

In Zurich the first believers are rebaptized against the state church, launching the movement later called Anabaptist, while Zwingli teaches a memorial understanding of the Supper, and the two great questions of the sacraments are reopened for the whole Western church.

At the Marburg Colloquy Luther and Zwingli meet to unite the Reformation and agree on fourteen of fifteen articles before breaking on the fifteenth, the presence of Christ at the table, with Luther refusing to move from the plain words this is my body, and the Protestant movement splits at the meal it hoped would join it.

John Calvin publishes the first edition of his Institutes, later developing an account of the Supper between Zwingli and Luther, confessing that believers truly feed on Christ by the Holy Spirit, a spiritual real presence received by faith.

The Council of Trent reaffirms transubstantiation dogmatically against the Reformers, hardening the confessional lines on the Supper, while Protestant confessions such as the later Westminster and Baptist statements set out the paedobaptist and credobaptist positions that endure to this day.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here, because we are taking up the two subjects the church has argued over longest, and it takes a certain courage to do that honestly. Before we start, three things. First, the goal of this study is not to win the argument. It is to understand what these signs are and to hold our convictions with humility, so we are going to make a rule together, that before anyone critiques a position they do not hold, they have to be able to state it in its strongest form, the way its own best defenders would. Second, we are going to keep a clear line between what the faith stands or falls on, which is not up for debate in this room, and what faithful churches disagree on and remain one, which is most of what we will discuss. You can disagree with the person next to you about baptism or the table and still be brothers and sisters, and we will act like it. Third, the writer is a Baptist and says so plainly, and he still works hard to state every other side fairly, and so will we, whatever tradition each of us brings. One more thing that matters. If anyone here has never been baptized, or has been made afraid of the communion table, this study is an invitation to you and not a debate to survive, and I am glad to talk privately anytime. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this session says. Now let us bring it home, off the map of positions and into how each of us actually comes to the water and the table, because none of this matters if it stays an argument about the sacraments in general and never touches the way we ourselves receive them.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not all resolved, because the church has held some of these questions in tension for two thousand years and we will not settle them in an evening, and the writer does not tie a bow on it either. Take the weight of this home with you. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. If tonight raised a question about your own baptism or your own place at the table, do not carry it alone, come find me. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the honesty it took to hold these things without turning into teams, which is harder and better than winning.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rule about steelmanning every view and the line between first-order and second-order matters, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Why God Gave Us Water and Bread, the goodness of matter and the sacrament and ordinance traditions.
Week 3: Session 2, Baptism: The Sign at the Door, part one, the shared meaning of baptism and the believer-baptism case at its strongest.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, the infant-baptism case at its strongest, where the writer lands, and the practice of reading the other side fairly.
Week 5: Session 3, Buried and Raised, union with Christ and the new identity of Romans 6, with extra time for anyone carrying shame.
Week 6: Session 4, What Happens at the Table, part one, the four views stated at their strongest.
Week 7: Session 4 continued, where the writer lands and the grief over a divided table, plus session 5's opening on the misreading of examine yourself.
Week 8: Session 5, The Table That Makes Us One, the corporate meaning of 1 Corinthians 11, and an integration close in the meal that makes a divided people one.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Why God Gave Us Water and Bread, the goodness of matter and the two traditions.
Week 2: Session 2, Baptism: The Sign at the Door, both cases stated at their strongest and the second-order verdict.
Week 3: Sessions 3 and 4 together, baptism as new identity in Romans 6 and the four views of the table.
Week 4: Session 5, The Table That Makes Us One, plus a short integration close in the water and the meal that mark and feed the church.

plan: Week 1: Session 1, Why God Gave Us Water and Bread.

Week 4: Session 4, What Happens at the Table.

bibliography.title: Christ, Baptism and the Lord's Supper: Recovering the Sacraments for Evangelical Worship
bibliography.author: Leonard J. Vander Zee
bibliography.note: An accessible evangelical recovery of the sacraments that takes both signs seriously without leaving the Protestant frame, useful across all five sessions for its fair handling of the traditions. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them as the study's own.

bibliography.title: The Lord's Supper: Eternal Word in Broken Bread
bibliography.author: Robert Letham
bibliography.note: A concise Reformed account of the Supper that fairly represents the memorial, Lutheran, Roman, and Calvinist positions before defending a spiritual real presence, the closest single book to where the study lands in session 4. Leader to confirm specifics.

bibliography.title: Baptism in the Early Church: History, Theology, and Liturgy in the First Five Centuries
bibliography.author: Everett Ferguson
bibliography.note: A magisterial study of early baptismal practice, cited in the timeline and in session 2's history, whose conclusions the credobaptist presses and the paedobaptist contests. Offered so leaders can weigh the historical evidence honestly rather than assume it.

bibliography.title: Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation
bibliography.author: James K. A. Smith
bibliography.note: The argument that human beings are formed less by ideas than by embodied practices and habits, supporting session 1's case for why God gives physical signs. Leader to test against Scripture and confirm before pressing specific claims.

bibliography.title: The First Apology
bibliography.author: Justin Martyr
bibliography.note: The second-century defense of the faith that describes the early church's baptism and weekly meal, cited in the timeline as a window into how the young church practiced the signs. A primary source, to be read rather than only quoted.

bibliography.title: The Didache: The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
bibliography.author: unknown, early church
bibliography.note: The earliest church manual, giving instructions for baptism and the thanksgiving meal, cited in session 2's history. Read by both baptism traditions, and honestly ambiguous on infants, which is itself worth noting to a group.

bibliography.title: On Christian Doctrine and related works
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The source of the enduring definition of a sacrament as a visible word, cited in session 1 and the timeline. Leader to handle with care, honoring the insight while noting the tradition's later disputes over what the signs convey.

bibliography.title: The First Epistle to the Corinthians (New International Commentary on the New Testament)
bibliography.author: Gordon D. Fee
bibliography.note: The standard evangelical commentary behind sessions 4 and 5, especially on the social setting of the Corinthian table and the meaning of discerning the body. Leader to confirm specific exegetical claims.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 4
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Calvin's treatment of baptism and the Supper, the source of the spiritual-presence view the study lands closest to in session 4 and the doctrine of union with Christ behind session 3. A primary text, weighty and rewarding, cited directly.

bibliography.title: The Meal Jesus Gave Us: Understanding Holy Communion
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A short, warm introduction to the Lord's Supper for ordinary Christians, useful background for sessions 4 and 5 and for the theme of the table as foretaste of the kingdom feast. Leader to confirm before attributing specific arguments.

bibliography.title: Baptism: Three Views
bibliography.author: David F. Wright, editor
bibliography.note: A multi-author volume in which advocates of believer's baptism, infant baptism, and a dual-practice position state and defend their cases directly, the ideal resource for a group wanting each baptism view in the words of its own best defenders. Session 2 background.

furtherReading: Christ, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, Leonard Vander Zee, for readers who want the fuller evangelical recovery of both signs behind the whole study.

Baptism: Three Views, edited by David F. Wright, for anyone wanting to read the believer-baptism and infant-baptism cases in the words of their own best defenders, the exact discipline session 2 asks for.
The Lord's Supper, Robert Letham, for readers who want the four views of the table laid out and weighed, closest to where session 4 lands, read as one careful voice among several.
Desiring the Kingdom, James K. A. Smith, for those who want the case that we are formed by embodied practice, behind session 1, read as common grace to be tested against Scripture.
1 Corinthians 10 and 11, read straight through, for anyone willing to sit with Paul's own teaching on the one bread and the divided table that grounds sessions 4 and 5.

glossary.definition: In the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions, a sign instituted by Christ that not only points to grace but is a means through which God conveys it. Augustine's lasting phrase is a visible word, an invisible grace given a form you can see and touch.

In many Baptist and free-church traditions, a practice the Lord ordained and commanded, an act of obedience and public proclamation, deliberately careful never to locate a saving power in the water or the bread themselves. The emphasis the study calls cautious in its words.

A channel through which God gives grace to his people, such as the preached word, prayer, and, in the sacramental traditions, baptism and the Supper. The ordinance instinct guards against making the sign work mechanically, apart from faith in Christ.

Believer's baptism, the conviction that baptism should be received by those who can profess faith, following the New Testament pattern of preaching, faith, and then the sign. The position the writer holds, as a Baptist, and treats as second-order.

Infant baptism, the conviction that the covenant sign belongs on the children of believers before they can profess faith, as circumcision was placed on Israel's children, grounded in covenant continuity and the priority of grace. Stated in the study at its strongest.

The paedobaptist argument that Scripture is one covenant of grace across both Testaments, so the sign moves from circumcision to baptism while its recipients, the children of believers, remain the same. The strongest objection the writer names but does not fully answer.

The doctrine at the heart of Romans 6, that the believer is so joined to Christ that his death and resurrection count as theirs, buried out of an old identity and raised into a new one. The truest thing about a Christian, given rather than achieved.

Associated with Zwingli, the understanding that this is my body means this represents my body, and that the Supper is a profound act of remembrance uniting the church around the cross. Guards the finished sacrifice and the danger of magic.

Associated with Calvin, the confession that Christ is truly and really present at the table, not in the elements but to faith, so that by the Spirit the believer genuinely feeds on the crucified and risen Christ. The view the study lands closest to.

The Lutheran confession, loosely called consubstantiation, that Christ's true body and blood are really present in, with, and under the bread and wine, received by the mouth, while the bread remains genuinely bread. Luther's refusal to soften the word is.

The Roman Catholic teaching, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 and Trent in 1551, that the substance of the bread and wine is changed entirely into the body and blood of Christ while the outward appearances remain. Guards, most intensely of all, the reality of Christ's presence.

The broad conviction, shared in different forms by the Lutheran, Roman, and Reformed traditions, that Christ is genuinely present at the table and not merely remembered. The study notes that three of the four views cluster far closer than the history of division suggests.

Paul's phrase in 1 Corinthians 11, which the study argues means recognizing the church, the many members who are one body, and not only reverencing the bread. To fail to discern the body is to despise the people Christ died to gather.

A matter worth studying, deciding, and holding with conviction, on which faithful churches disagree while remaining one in the faith, as opposed to first-order doctrines the creeds bind. Baptism and the Supper are second-order, real but not walls between Christians.

Built so anyone can lead it with no prep. Come to understand, not to win.
